## Where we are

| Model | Determinism | Time | State |
|---|---|---|---|
| ODE (Day 1) | deterministic | continuous | continuous |
| Function map (Day 1) | deterministic | discrete | continuous |
| Markov chain (Day 1) | stochastic | discrete | discrete |
| **Jump process (now)** | **stochastic** | **continuous** | **discrete** |

All four are population models: the state is counts, not people.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes at the start of the day. These four axes are the map the whole
course is drawn on, and today fills in the last population-level corner:
stochastic, continuous in time, discrete in state. Point out that the
individual-level column is still empty; that is Day 3.
:::

## Why events matter

- A CTMC waits for the next infection or recovery.
- The state is integer-valued: $X=(S,I,R)$.
- Exact event timing exposes fade-out and peak variability.

For the baseline population,
$$
a_{\mathrm{inf}}=\frac{\beta cSI}{N},\qquad
a_{\mathrm{rec}}=\gamma I.
$$

::: {.notes}
Contrast this with an ODE: an ODE advances all flows over a numerical
interval, while a jump process samples the next event and its type.
:::

## Recap: where the exponential comes from

An event with constant hazard $r$ has waiting time $T$ with

$$
\Pr(T>t)=e^{-rt},\qquad \Pr(T\le\delta t)=1-e^{-r\delta t},
$$

the same conversion used for the discrete-time chain on Day 1.

::: {.notes}
Five minutes, no derivation on the board. Point out that the survival function
is where yesterday's rate-to-proportion rule came from: the per-step
probability is the chance the waiting time lands inside the step. The full
derivation is in the probability prerequisite; nobody needs to have read it to
follow this session.
:::

## Recap: memoryless clocks and which one rings first

Exponential waiting times are **memoryless**,

$$
\Pr(T>s+t\mid T>s)=e^{-rt}=\Pr(T>t),
$$

so no per-individual clock has to be carried and the counts $(S,I,R)$ are the
whole state. With competing events at rates $a_j$ and $a_0=\sum_j a_j$,

$$
\min_j T_j\sim\operatorname{Exponential}(a_0),
\qquad \Pr(J=j)=\frac{a_j}{a_0}.
$$

::: {.notes}
Memorylessness is a real assumption about the disease: someone infectious for a
week is no closer to recovering than someone infected this morning. The two
displayed results are the whole Gillespie algorithm: when the next event
happens, and which one it is. The next slide is bookkeeping rather than new
mathematics. Learners who want the derivations should read the waiting-times
section of the probability prerequisite afterwards.
:::

## Gillespie direct algorithm

At state $x$, let $a_0=a_{\mathrm{inf}}+a_{\mathrm{rec}}$.

1. Draw $\tau\sim\operatorname{Exponential}(a_0)$.
2. Choose infection with probability $a_{\mathrm{inf}}/a_0$.
3. Apply $(-1,+1,0)$ or $(0,-1,+1)$.

This is a stochastic, continuous-time, discrete-state, population-level
model.  Every event conserves $S+I+R=N$.

::: {.notes}
The propensities are rates, not probabilities.  The waiting time is continuous
even though the state changes by integer increments.
:::

## A visible Julia kernel

```{julia}
using Random, StableRNGs

function gillespie_sir(N, I₀, β, c, γ, tmax, rng)
    t, x = 0.0, [N - I₀, I₀, 0]
    times, states = [t], [copy(x)]
    while t < tmax && x[2] > 0
        a = (β*c*x[1]*x[2]/N, γ*x[2])
        a₀ = sum(a)
        a₀ == 0 && break
        t += randexp(rng)/a₀
        t > tmax && break
        if rand(rng)*a₀ < a[1]
            x[1] -= 1; x[2] += 1
        else
            x[2] -= 1; x[3] += 1
        end
        push!(times, t); push!(states, copy(x))
    end
    (; times, states)
end
```

::: {.notes}
The state update is the stoichiometric change vector in code.  The local
StableRNG makes the result reproducible without relying on global state.
:::

## One path, and the ODE through it

```{julia}
#| label: fig-slide-ch04-path
#| fig-cap: "One exact CTMC path (steps) against the mean-field ODE (dashed)."
using CairoMakie, OrdinaryDiffEq

path = gillespie_sir(1000, 10, 0.05, 10.0, 0.25, 40.0,
    StableRNG(20250711))
states = reduce(hcat, path.states)
@assert maximum(abs.(sum(states; dims=1) .- 1000)) == 0   # conservation

function sir_drift!(du, u, p, t)
    κ, γ = p
    du[1] = -κ*u[1]*u[2]
    du[2] =  κ*u[1]*u[2] - γ*u[2]
    du[3] =  γ*u[2]
end
grid = collect(0.0:0.2:40.0)
ode = Array(solve(ODEProblem(sir_drift!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], (0.0, 40.0),
    (0.05*10/1000, 0.25)), Tsit5(); saveat = grid))

fig = Figure(size = (900, 380))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "people",
    title = "$(length(path.times)-1) events, peak I = $(maximum(states[2, :]))")
for (j, (name, col)) in enumerate(zip(["S", "I", "R"],
        [:steelblue, :firebrick, :seagreen]))
    stairs!(ax, path.times, states[j, :]; color = col, linewidth = 2,
        label = "$name (jump)")
    lines!(ax, grid, ode[j, :]; color = col, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 1.5)
end
axislegend(ax, position = :rc)
fig
```

::: {.notes}
This is the picture the whole morning is about. Every wiggle is a real event, and
at a thousand people there are well over a thousand of them, so the steps merge
into a rough curve. Zooming in on the first few days is where you would see
individual jumps. The dashed curves are yesterday's model, and the gap is not
solver error: this particular realization ran a few days late, and a
different seed would run early.

The title numbers are generated at render time and are realization-specific;
conservation is asserted, so a broken kernel would fail the render. Do not let
anyone read one path as an expected epidemic; that is the next two slides.
:::

## Recap: two kinds of spread

For $M$ independent paths with summary values $z_1,\dots,z_M$,

$$
\bar z=\frac1M\sum_k z_k,\qquad
s^2=\frac1{M-1}\sum_k (z_k-\bar z)^2,\qquad
\operatorname{se}(\bar z)=\frac{s}{\sqrt M}.
$$

- The standard deviation $s$ describes **the epidemics**: how much peak size
  varies. More simulation does not shrink it.
- The standard error $\operatorname{se}(\bar z)$ describes **our estimate** of
  the average, and does shrink, as $1/\sqrt M$: four times the work to halve it.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes, and it pays for itself four times today. These two spreads get
confused constantly, so keep them apart: one is a property of the disease
process, the other a property of how hard we simulated. Say explicitly that this
is the vocabulary the rest of the day uses. The relative spread of SDE peaks
after the break, the variance-to-mean ratio of case counts this afternoon, and
the variance decomposition in the last session all live on this slide. Nobody
needs the probability prerequisite for it.
:::

## From model to package API

The same reaction structure, in current SciML packages, executed here:

```{julia}
#| label: ch04-catalyst
using Catalyst, JumpProcesses

sir_network = @reaction_network begin
    κ, S + I --> 2I
    γ, I --> R
end
u₀ = [:S => 990, :I => 10, :R => 0]
jump_parameters = [:κ => 0.05*10/1000, :γ => 0.25]

function simulate_jump(seed)
    problem = JumpProblem(sir_network, u₀, (0.0, 40.0), jump_parameters;
        aggregator = Direct(), rng = StableRNG(seed))
    return Array(solve(problem, SSAStepper(); saveat = grid)(grid))
end
size(simulate_jump(3001))
```

One rate constant per reaction, so the $\beta cSI/N$ above becomes $\kappa SI$
with $\kappa=\beta c/N$; $R_0=\beta c/\gamma=2$ is unchanged.

::: {.notes}
Two reactions in two lines, against the hand-written kernel three slides back.
Say that out loud rather than reading the code. The kappa note matters because
the book chapter uses kappa from here on: a reaction network carries one rate
constant per reaction, and the baseline scenario has not changed. The network
also records stoichiometry explicitly, which is what lets the same object become
an ODE, an SDE, or a jump model later in the course.
:::

## Twenty paths and the ODE

```{julia}
#| label: fig-slide-ch04-ensemble
#| fig-cap: "Twenty CTMC paths of infectious prevalence with the mean-field ODE."
using Statistics

M = 20
ensemble = cat((simulate_jump(3000 + k) for k in 1:M)...; dims = 3)
peaks = [maximum(ensemble[2, :, k]) for k in 1:M]

fig2 = Figure(size = (900, 380))
ax2 = Axis(fig2[1, 1], xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "infectious",
    title = "peak I: mean $(round(Int, mean(peaks))), sd $(round(Int, std(peaks)))" *
            ", se $(round(std(peaks)/sqrt(M); digits = 1))")
for k in 1:M
    lines!(ax2, grid, ensemble[2, :, k]; color = (:firebrick, 0.35), linewidth = 1)
end
lines!(ax2, grid, ode[2, :]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 2.5)
fig2
```

::: {.notes}
Five minutes, and let them look before you talk. Two things to point at. First
the spread in *timing*: every path has the same shape but peaks somewhere between
roughly day 13 and day 25. Second, and this is the one worth labouring: the
dashed ODE is not the average of the paths. Its peak is near 158 while the mean
of the twenty individual peak heights is around 178, because each path peaks at
its own time and averaging asynchronous peaks flattens the curve. So "the ODE
peak" and "the average peak of an epidemic" are different quantities.

The three numbers in the title are the previous slide made concrete: sd is the
epidemics varying, se is how well twenty runs pin the average down. Note that
none of these twenty paths fades out. With ten initial infectives and $R_0=2$
that is expected, since fade-out needs all ten introductions to fail. Fade-out is
a small-introduction phenomenon, and the worksheet quantifies it.
:::

## Takeaways and links

- Propensities determine both waiting times and event probabilities.
- Exact jumps preserve integer states and population conservation.
- Ensemble summaries are needed for comparison with an ODE.
